Evidence for:
- The paper concludes that six months of physical activity produced a modest cognitive improvement in adults with subjective memory impairment over an 18-month follow-up; this supports the claim for that population. [S:5191b631229c#15]
- Participants were randomly assigned to a 24-week home-based physical activity program or education and usual care. [S:5191b631229c#9]
- The primary outcome was change in ADAS-Cog scores over 18 months; the intervention–control difference at intervention completion was −1.3 points (95% CI, −2.38 to −0.22), with the interval excluding zero. [S:5191b631229c#10] [S:5191b631229c#12]

Evidence against and limitations:
- Follow-up was incomplete: 170 participants were randomized, and 138 completed the 18-month assessment. [S:5191b631229c#8]
- The supplied passages do not report separate within-group baseline changes or other cognitive outcomes, so those aspects cannot be assessed from this evidence. [S:5191b631229c#10] [S:5191b631229c#12]
- The conclusion concerns adults with subjective memory impairment and describes the improvement as modest; it does not establish the same benefit for everyone. [S:5191b631229c#15]

[S:6d01e1e4d839#6] [S:6d01e1e4d839#7]
- It reports a significant correlation after controlling for chronological age and sex (14079881.pdf, p. 1: “Perceived age, controlled for chronological age and sex, also correlated significantly with physical and cognitive functioning as well as with leucocyte telomere length.”). [S:6d01e1e4d839#12]

Evidence against or limiting the claim:
- The supplied correlation passage gives neither its direction nor its magnitude; statistical significance alone does not establish that cellular ageing “closely” links to older appearance (14079881.pdf, p. 1: “correlated significantly with physical and cognitive functioning as well as with leucocyte telomere length”). [S:6d01e1e4d839#12]
- The paper is a cohort study involving 1826 twins aged 70 or older, which limits the population directly represented by this evidence (14079881.pdf, p. 1: “cohort study”; “1826 twins aged >or=70”). [S:6d01e1e4d839#1] [S:6d01e1e4d839#5]
- The supplied telomere result reports adjustment for chronological age and sex; the additional adjustment for rearing environment concerns survival, so it cannot establish broader confounder control for the telomere association (14079881.pdf, p. 1: “Perceived age, controlled for chronological age and sex”; “perceived age was significantly associated with survival, even after adjustment for chronological age, sex, and rearing environment”). [S:6d01e1e4d839#12] [S:6d01e1e4d839#8]

The excerpts support an association between perceived age and one molecular ageing marker, but do not establish the strength or direction needed to substantiate the claim as worded (14079881.pdf, p. 1: “correlated significantly ... with leucocyte telomere length”). [S:6d01e1e4d839#12]

The paper explicitly claims state-of-the-art KBQA accuracy on **SimpleQuestions** (single-relation) and **WebQSP** (multi-relation), but its detailed results qualify the WebQSP claim. In 1704.06194.pdf, p. 1: “it helps our KBQA system achieve state-of-the-art accuracy for both single-relation (SimpleQuestions) and multi-relation (WebQSP) QA benchmarks.” [S:cff40022c0ad#4]

- **SimpleQuestions:** The top-3 relation-detector configuration achieves a new state of the art; **WebQSP:** that configuration is described as comparable to the state of the art. In 1704.06194.pdf, p. 9: “we also try to use the top-3 relation detectors from Section 6.2” and report “a new state-of-the-art result on SimpleQuestions and a result comparable to the state-of-the-art on WebQSP.” [S:cff40022c0ad#104]
- **Evaluation settings:** SimpleQuestions uses FB2M and prior entity-linking results; WebQSP uses the entire Freebase KB and S-MART entity linking. In 1704.06194.pdf, p. 7: “The KB we use consists of a Freebase subset with 2M entities (FB2M)”; “For the KBQA evaluation, we also start with their entity linking results”; “We use the entire Freebase KB for evaluation purposes”; and “we use S-MART (Yang and Chang, 2015) entity-linking outputs.” [S:cff40022c0ad#85]
- **Separate relation-detection results:** HR-BiLSTM achieves 93.3% accuracy on SimpleQuestions and 82.53% on WebQSP test sets; these are relation-detection scores, rather than end-to-end KBQA scores. In 1704.06194.pdf, p. 8, the model row reads “Hier-Res-BiLSTM (HR-BiLSTM) words + rel names 93.3 82.53,” and the caption states “Accuracy on the SimpleQuestions and WebQSP relation detection tasks (test sets).” [S:cff40022c0ad#91]

Relation detection is a core component of
many NLP applications including Knowl-
edge Base Question Answering (KBQA).
In this paper, we propose a hierarchi-
cal recurrent neural network enhanced by
residual learning which detects KB re-

Our
method uses deep residual bidirectional
LSTMs to compare questions and rela-
tion names via different levels of abstrac-

ple KBQA system that integrates entity
linking and our proposed relation detec-

each other. Our experimental results show
that our approach not only achieves out-
standing relation detection performance,
but more importantly, it helps our KBQA
system achieve state-of-the-art accuracy
for both single-relation (SimpleQuestions)
and multi-relation (WebQSP) QA bench-
marks.

answer:
The proposed framework combines a Hierarchical Residual BiLSTM (HR-BiLSTM) relation detector with a knowledge-base question-answering (KBQA) pipeline. The model is explicitly named in 1704.06194.pdf, p.5: “The proposed Hierarchical Residual BiLSTM (HR-BiLSTM) model for relation detection.” [S:3a22a6ddc6dc#48]

- **Relation representations:** It uses both whole-relation and word-level representations, encoded with shared-parameter BiLSTMs and combined through max-pooling (1704.06194.pdf, p.2: “we propose to build both relation-level and word-level relation representations”; p.4: “use two BiLSTMs (with shared parameters)” and “We apply one max-pooling on these two sets of vectors and get the ﬁnal relation representation hr.”). [S:3a22a6ddc6dc#19] [S:3a22a6ddc6dc#43]
- **Question encoding and matching:** It uses deep bidirectional LSTMs, residual shortcut connections between two layers, max-pooling, and cosine similarity to match questions with relations (1704.06194.pdf, p.2: “we use deep bidirectional LSTMs (BiLSTMs) to learn different levels of question representations”; p.5: “adding shortcut connections between two BiLSTM layers” and “Finally we compute the matching score of r given q as srel(r; q) = cos(hr, hq).”). [S:3a22a6ddc6dc#19] [S:3a22a6ddc6dc#53]
- **KBQA pipeline:** It uses initial entity linking, relation-based entity re-ranking, core relation or relation-chain detection, query formation, and optional constraint detection (1704.06194.pdf, p.2: “Given an input question and a set of candidate entities retrieved by an entity linker”; “Re-ranking the entity candidates”; “Finding the core relation (chains)”; “an optional constraint detection step”; and “Based on the detected entity and relation, we form a query to search the KB”). [S:3a22a6ddc6dc#19] [S:3a22a6ddc6dc#20] [S:3a22a6ddc6dc#18]
- **Constraint handling:** It uses text matching over a generated KB subgraph, comparing question n-grams with neighboring entity names (1704.06194.pdf, p.7: “we adopt an additional constraint detection step based on text matching” and “we compute a matching score between each n-gram in the input question ... and entity name of c”). [S:3a22a6ddc6dc#80]
- **Knowledge resources and entity linkers:** For SimpleQuestions, it uses the FB2M Freebase subset and entity-linking results from Yin et al.; for WebQSP, it uses the entire Freebase KB and S-MART entity-linking outputs (1704.06194.pdf, p.7: “a Freebase subset with 2M entities (FB2M)”; “we also start with their entity linking results”; “We use the entire Freebase KB for evaluation purposes”; and “we use S-MART (Yang and Chang, 2015) entity-linking outputs.”). [S:3a22a6ddc6dc#85]

answer:
The paper uses three evaluation metrics, introduced on page 4 of **1708.01464.pdf** with: “We use the following three evaluation metrics:” [S:adecdb59a660#39]

- **Phoneme Error Rate (PER):** Levenshtein distance between predicted and gold phoneme sequences, divided by the gold sequence length. The definition on page 4 states: “Phoneme Error Rate (PER) is the Lev- enshtein distance between the predicted phoneme sequences and the gold standard phoneme sequences, divided by the length of the gold standard phoneme sequences.” [S:adecdb59a660#40]
- **Word Error Rate (WER):** Percentage of words whose predicted phoneme sequence fails to match the gold sequence exactly. Page 4 states: “Word Error Rate (WER) is the percentage of words in which the predicted phoneme se- quence does not exactly match the gold stan- dard phoneme sequence.” [S:adecdb59a660#41]
- **Word Error Rate 100 (WER 100):** Percentage of test words whose correct pronunciation is absent from the system’s first 100 guesses. Page 4 states: “Word Error Rate 100 (WER 100) is the per- centage of words in the test set for which the correct guess is not in the ﬁrst 100 guesses of the system.” [S:adecdb59a660#42]

answer:
The paper introduces a paragraph-level neural model that predicts discourse relations between adjacent discourse units using two Bi-LSTM layers, max pooling and a softmax prediction layer, with a CRF extension to model relation sequences (1804.05918.pdf, pp. 3 and 2: “consists of two Bi-LSTM layers, one max-pooling layer in between and one softmax prediction layer”; “we add a CRF layer on top of the discourse relation prediction layer”). [S:48ab631afb87#21] [S:48ab631afb87#11]

**Reported improvement over previous state of the art:** in binary implicit-relation classification, the model with untied prediction parameters improves F1 by approximately **6 points for Comparison and 7 points for Temporal** (1804.05918.pdf, p. 8: “compared against the best previous systems” and “F1-score improve- ments of 6 points on Comparison and 7 points on Temporal”). [S:48ab631afb87#88] The supplied evidence does not include the underlying binary scores or the previous-best multiclass scores, so exact score-to-score state-of-the-art comparisons cannot be established.

**Available multiclass scores:** the full ensemble achieves **51.84 macro F1 / 59.75 accuracy for implicit relations** and **94.17 macro F1 / 94.82 accuracy for explicit relations** (1804.05918.pdf, p. 8, Table 5: “+ the CRF Layer 51.84 59.75 94.17 94.82”). [S:48ab631afb87#82] Its macro-F1 gains over the paper’s corresponding single model are **3.02 points implicit** and **0.96 points explicit**, which are ensemble gains rather than comparisons with previous state of the art (1804.05918.pdf, p. 8: “combine results of ten runs” and “(51.84 - 48.82 = 3.02) and (94.17 - 93.21 = 0.96)”). [S:48ab631afb87#89]

**Evaluation qualifications:** the experiments use PDTB v2.0’s four top-level classes—Comparison, Contingency, Expansion and Temporal—with sections 2–20 for training, 21–22 for testing and 0–1 for development (1804.05918.pdf, p. 5: “Comparison (Comp), Contingency (Cont), Expansion (Exp) and Temporal (Temp)” and “sections 2- 20 as training set, sections 21-22 as test set, and sections 0-1 as development set”). [S:48ab631afb87#49] Binary evaluation trains separate one-versus-all classifiers, while the main evaluation uses four-way classification; the CRF is unsuitable for binary classification (1804.05918.pdf, p. 7: “separate ‘one- versus-all’ binary classifiers were trained” and “mainly evaluate our proposed models using the four-way multi-class classification setting”; p. 8: “the CRF layer of the model is not suitable for binary classification”). [S:48ab631afb87#75] [S:48ab631afb87#76] [S:48ab631afb87#88] The authors report ten-run averages for their individual models and baselines, whereas many previous works reported their best performance, which qualifies the comparison (1804.05918.pdf, p. 6: “report the average performance of each model in- stead of the best performance as reported in many previous works”). [S:48ab631afb87#63]

answer:
The paper evaluated three NER models in **1810.08699.pdf**:

- **Stanford NER**, a feature-based conditional random field (CRF) baseline (p. 4: “Stanford NER is conditional random ﬁelds (CRF) classiﬁer based on lexical and contextual features”). [S:9f6610241fbf#44]
- **spaCy 2.0**, a CNN-based transition-system baseline (p. 4: “spaCy 2.0 uses a CNN-based transition system for named entity recognition”). [S:9f6610241fbf#44]
- **Char-biLSTM+biLSTM+CRF**, the main recurrent model: character-level bidirectional LSTM representations are concatenated with word vectors, passed through another bidirectional LSTM, and labeled by a CRF (p. 4: “The main model that we focused on was the recurrent model with a CRF top layer”; p. 5: “TABLE IV: Evaluation results for Char-biLSTM+biLSTM+CRF”). [S:9f6610241fbf#48] [S:9f6610241fbf#53]

**Variants:** Both neural models were evaluated with 50-, 100-, 200-, and 300-dimensional GloVe embeddings; 50 dimensions worked best for the recurrent model and 200 for spaCy (p. 5: “GloVe word vector models of four different sizes (50, 100, 200, and 300) were tested, with vectors of size 50 producing the best results (Table IV). For spaCy 2.0 named entity recognizer, the same word embedding models were tested. However, in this case the per- formance of 200-dimensional embeddings was highest (Table V).”). [S:9f6610241fbf#55]

**Results tables:** Table III compares the evaluated algorithms, Table IV covers Char-biLSTM+biLSTM+CRF, and Table V covers spaCy 2.0 (p. 5: “TABLE III: Evaluation results for named entity recognition algorithms”; “TABLE IV: Evaluation results for Char-biLSTM+biLSTM+CRF”; “TABLE V: Evaluation results for spaCy 2.0 NER”). The supplied evidence includes these captions but not the tables’ numerical cells, so exact scores cannot be reported. [S:9f6610241fbf#52] [S:9f6610241fbf#53] [S:9f6610241fbf#54]

The supplied evidence identifies the static vectors as **principal-component (PC) embeddings derived from contextualized representations**, with embeddings created separately from different layers; however, it does not provide the extraction passage needed to establish exactly which component is used or how it is calculated (1909.00512.pdf, p. 8: “For all three contextualizing models, PC static embeddings created from lower layers are more effec- tive those created from upper layers.”). [S:5acb038c7127#67]

For layer selection, the authors report that BERT’s first layer produces the best-performing PC static embeddings (1909.00512.pdf, p. 8: “The best-performing PC static embeddings be- long to the ﬁrst layer of BERT”). [S:5acb038c7127#67]

For context collection, their analysis uses SemEval Semantic Textual Similarity data from 2012–2016 and maps each word to its sentences and positions within them (1909.00512.pdf, p. 3: “Our input data come from the SemEval Semantic Textual Similarity tasks from years 2012 - 2016”; “Using these datasets, we map words to the list of sen- tences they appear in and their index within these sentences.”). [S:5acb038c7127#21]

The provided evidence is insufficient to specify the static-embedding procedure’s occurrence sampling, averaging, PCA implementation, or output dimensionality; the context-collection passage alone does not establish those details.

answer:
The corpus includes the following typography information and related annotations:

- **Font type and style for individual tokens**, including italics and bold print, plus token positions on physical pages for PDFs; these are attributes of token elements (1909.09067.pdf, p. 6: “Information on the font type and font style (e.g., italics, bold print) of a token and its po- sition on the physical page (for PDFs only) was speciﬁed as attributes to the token ele- ments of the tokens layer”). [S:ff482f66ff87#56]
- **Detailed font configurations in a separate fonts layer**, referenced from the tokens layer (1909.09067.pdf, p. 6: “A separate fonts layer was introduced to preserve detailed information on the font con- ﬁgurations referenced in the tokens layer”). [S:ff482f66ff87#59] The XML example records font ID, name, full name, type, embedding status, ascender, cap height, italic angle, descender, weight, and x-height (1909.09067.pdf, p. 7: `<font id="F0" name="TradeGothic-BoldTwo" fullname="UDSPGZ+TradeGothic-BoldTwo" type="Type 1 CFF" embedded="true" ascender="977" capheight="722" italicangle="0" descender="-229" weight="700" xheight="520"/>`). [S:ff482f66ff87#68]
- **Related layout annotations** cover paragraph and line segmentation, plus physical page segmentation for PDFs, represented through textspan elements in the textstructure layer (1909.09067.pdf, p. 6: “Information on physical page segmenta- tion (for PDFs only), paragraph segmen- tation, and line segmentation was added as part of a textspan element in the textstructure layer”). [S:ff482f66ff87#57]

The paper describes collection, representation, and use as follows:

- **Collection:** HTML cleanup used Python’s Beautiful Soup while retaining typography such as boldface and italics; PDF extraction used PDFlib TET to record typography alongside text structure and images in TETML XML (1909.09067.pdf, p. 3: “HTML markup and boilerplate removed using the Beautiful Soup library for Python”; “typography (e.g., boldface, italics) was retained”; “For PDFs, the PDFlib Text and Image Extrac- tion Toolkit (TET) was used to extract the plain text and record information on text structure, ty- pography, and images”; “The toolkit produces out- put in an XML format (TETML)”). [S:ff482f66ff87#30]
- **Representation:** annotations use Text Corpus Format (TCF), with the source text and annotation layers stored together and linked through tokens (1909.09067.pdf, p. 5: “Annotations were added in the Text Corpus Format by WebLicht (TCF)”; p. 6: “the source text and all annotation layers are stored jointly in a single ﬁle. A token layer acts as the key element to which all other annotation layers are linked”). [S:ff482f66ff87#53] [S:ff482f66ff87#55]
- **Use:** a reported study found structural features, including counts of words of a particular font type, predictive of simplified German text difficulty (1909.09067.pdf, p. 6: “number of words of a speciﬁc font type, and adherence to a one-sentence-per-line rule) to be predictive of the level of difﬁculty of a simpliﬁed German text”). [S:ff482f66ff87#64] The paper also proposes using typography information in neural machine translation for text simplification (1909.09067.pdf, p. 6: “Information on text structure, typography, and images can also be leveraged as part of a neu- ral machine translation approach to text simpli- ﬁcation”). [S:ff482f66ff87#65]

The main method is **PG-net**, identified as “pointer networks with coverage mechanism (PG-net)(See, Liu, and Manning 2017)” (2002.03407.pdf, p. 2). [S:e0ed96e9cc3d#24]

It uses an encoder–decoder with attention, pointer networks to address out-of-vocabulary words, and coverage to reduce repetition: “they used pointer networks to solve the out of vocabulary issue” and “used coverage mechanism to solve the problem of word repetition” (2002.03407.pdf, p. 1). [S:e0ed96e9cc3d#9]

The paper applies domain transfer to PG-net: “the model was pretrained using the CNN/DM dataset, then ﬁne tuned using the student reﬂection dataset” (2002.03407.pdf, p. 2). [S:e0ed96e9cc3d#24]

It also tests **Fast-RL**, described as “fast abstractive summarization with reinforcement learning,” but reports only PG-net experiments because “Fast-RL showed similar behavior to PG-net with lower performance” (2002.03407.pdf, p. 2). [S:e0ed96e9cc3d#25]

answer:
The original SQuAD contained **107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 Wikipedia articles**, while SQuAD 2.0 added **53,775 new unanswerable questions** about the same paragraphs; these counts measure the original question-answer collection and the added unanswerable questions, respectively (1606.05250v3.pdf, p. 2: “SQuAD contains 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 articles”; 1806.03822v1.pdf, p. 2: “with 53,775 new, unanswerable questions about the same paragraphs.”). [S:93a84fa7c6d6#12] [S:dae5a1d64c55#14]

In **1606.05250v3.pdf**, crowdworkers wrote questions about Wikipedia passages and selected answers from the passage text (p. 2: “questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles” and “the answer to every question is a segment of text, or span, from the corresponding reading passage.”). [S:93a84fa7c6d6#12]

The original annotation process asked workers to write and answer up to five questions per paragraph, highlight answers, and use their own wording (1606.05250v3.pdf, p. 4: “crowdworkers were tasked with asking and answering up to 5 questions”; “the answers had to be highlighted in the paragraph”; “crowdworkers were encouraged to ask questions in their own words”). [S:93a84fa7c6d6#42]

In **1806.03822v1.pdf**, the two challenging design properties of the new unanswerable questions are **paragraph relevance** and **a plausible answer of the requested type appearing in the paragraph** (p. 2: “Crowdworkers crafted these questions so that (1) they are relevant to the para- graph, and (2) the paragraph contains a plausible answer—something of the same type as what the question asks for.”). In SQuAD 2.0, a correct abstention on an unanswerable question receives 1 for both Exact Match and F1, while a nonempty answer receives 0 for both: 1806.03822v1.pdf, p. 4, states, “For negative examples, abstaining receives a score of 1, and any other response gets 0, for both exact match and F1.” [S:4a6240624a71#57]

For the reported test evaluation, the no-answer threshold is chosen separately for each model on the development set to maximize development-set F1: 1806.03822v1.pdf, p. 4, states, “We tune this threshold separately for each model on the development set. When evaluating on the test set, we use the threshold that maximizes F1 score on the development set.” [S:4a6240624a71#55]

The supplied evidence from 1606.05250v3.pdf does not include the original definitions of Exact Match or token-overlap F1, normalization, or handling of multiple reference answers. Those parts of the question—and a comparison of the papers’ metric definitions—cannot be answered from the provided evidence.

citations.claim: For reported SQuAD 2.0 test evaluation, the threshold is tuned separately for each model on the development set, maximizing development-set F1.
citations.quote:
We evaluated three existing model architectures:
the BiDAF-No-Answer (BNA) model proposed by
Levy et al. (2017), and two versions of the Docu-
mentQA No-Answer (DocQA) model from Clark
and Gardner (2017), namely versions with and
without ELMo (Peters et al., 2018). These mod-
els all learn to predict the probability that a ques-
tion is unanswerable, in addition to a distribution
over answer choices. At test time, models abstain
whenever their predicted probability that a ques-
tion is unanswerable exceeds some threshold. We
tune this threshold separately for each model on
the development set. When evaluating on the test
set, we use the threshold that maximizes F1 score
on the development set. We ﬁnd this strategy does
slightly better than simply taking the argmax pre-
diction, possibly due to the different proportions
of negative examples at training and test time.

- **ResNet — 1512.03385v1.pdf, page 7:** “We combine six models of different depth to form an ensemble (only with two 152-layer ones at the time of submitting). This leads to 3.57% top-5 error on the test set (Table 5).” [S:f59ad43fecc3#65]
- **ResNet evaluation — 1512.03385v1.pdf, page 4:** “In testing, for comparison studies we adopt the standard 10-crop testing [21].” This establishes the comparison-study protocol, but does not establish the competition ensemble’s evaluation protocol. [S:f59ad43fecc3#33]
- **DenseNet split and crops — 1608.06993v5.pdf, page 5:** “The ILSVRC 2012 classiﬁcation dataset [2] consists 1.2 million images for training, and 50,000 for val- idation, from 1, 000 classes.” It specifies “a single-crop or 10-crop with size 224×224 at test time” and states, “we report classiﬁcation errors on the validation set.” [S:9838a25ce21b#51]

**These results cannot establish a like-for-like head-to-head advantage:** ResNet’s quoted result uses six models on the test set, whereas DenseNet reports validation results with single-crop and 10-crop evaluation; the supplied evidence also leaves the competition ensemble’s evaluation protocol and DenseNet-201’s numerical entries unresolved. answer:
The supplied evidence is insufficient to establish the requested accuracy gap: it does not give the original ViT paper’s JFT-pretrained ViT-L/16 ImageNet top-1 result, and although DeiT reports 83.1%, the supplied passage does not explicitly tie that result to non-distilled DeiT-B at 384 resolution. The DeiT abstract states: “Our reference vision transformer (86M parameters) achieves top-1 accuracy of 83.1% (single-crop) on ImageNet with no external data” (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.1). [S:fc9a60595b40#4]

The data regimes differ: the original ViT paper lists ViT-L/16 under JFT-300M pretraining and describes ImageNet fine-tuning using the entire training set for final results; its scaling study includes L/16 pretrained for both seven and fourteen epochs (2010.11929v2.pdf, p.8: “L/16, pre-trained for 7 epochs, plus L/16 and H/14 pre-trained for 14 epochs”; p.13: “For ﬁnal results we train on the entire training set and evaluate on the respective test data”). [S:cf000b8c503b#82] [S:cf000b8c503b#171] DeiT uses ImageNet-1k alone (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.4: “with Imagenet1k only”). [S:fc9a60595b40#20]

These excerpts do not support assigning any accuracy difference to one design choice. Architecture is partly shared: DeiT says its reference DeiT-B “has the same architecture as ViT-B,” rather than establishing equivalence to the requested ViT-L/16; it also states, “we do not use a MLP head for the pre-training but only a linear classiﬁer” (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.8). [S:fc9a60595b40#48] Model size is incompletely documented here: the DeiT reference model has 86M parameters, but the supplied evidence does not provide ViT-L/16’s parameter count (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.1: “Our reference vision transformer (86M parameters)”). [S:fc9a60595b40#4]

Resolution and training procedure also require controls: DeiT describes “initial training at resolution 224×224” followed by “ﬁne-tuning at resolution 384×384” (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.15), whereas the supplied excerpts do not identify the resolution of the requested ViT-L/16 result. [S:fc9a60595b40#108] DeiT reports extensive augmentation and regularization, including “Regularization like Mixup [60] and Cutmix [59] improve performance” and “We also use repeated augmentation” (2012.12877v2.pdf, p.16); ViT states, “We ﬁne-tune all ViT models using SGD with a momentum of 0.9” (2010.11929v2.pdf, p.13). These data and procedure differences, together with missing matched size and resolution evidence, prevent a single-factor causal conclusion. [S:fc9a60595b40#117] [S:cf000b8c503b#171]

performing vision transformers are pre-trained with hundreds of millions
of images using a large infrastructure, thereby limiting their adoption.
In this work, we produce competitive convolution-free transformers by
training on Imagenet only. We train them on a single computer in less than
3 days. Our reference vision transformer (86M parameters) achieves top-1
accuracy of 83.1% (single-crop) on ImageNet with no external data.
More importantly, we introduce a teacher-student strategy speciﬁc to
transformers.

citations.quote:
We perform a controlled scaling study of different models by evaluating transfer performance from
JFT-300M. In this setting data size does not bottleneck the models’ performances, and we assess
performance versus pre-training cost of each model. The model set includes: 7 ResNets, R50x1,
R50x2 R101x1, R152x1, R152x2, pre-trained for 7 epochs, plus R152x2 and R200x3 pre-trained
for 14 epochs; 6 Vision Transformers, ViT-B/32, B/16, L/32, L/16, pre-trained for 7 epochs, plus
L/16 and H/14 pre-trained for 14 epochs; and 5 hybrids, R50+ViT-B/32, B/16, L/32, L/16 pre-
trained for 7 epochs, plus R50+ViT-L/16 pre-trained for 14 epochs (for hybrids, the number at the
end of the model name stands not for the patch size, but for the total dowsampling ratio in the ResNet
backbone).

answer:
In ViT, the learnable class token provides the final image representation used for classification; in DeiT, the class branch learns the true label, the distillation branch learns the teacher’s hard predicted label, and late fusion adds their softmax outputs. [S:d35d59fc5ce2#26] [S:cc5a543a8c6c#41] [S:cc5a543a8c6c#46]

- **ViT — 2010.11929v2.pdf, p. 3:** A learnable embedding is prepended to the patch sequence, and its final encoder state feeds the classification head: “whose state at the output of the Transformer encoder (z0 L) serves as the image representation y (Eq. 4).” The head is an MLP with one hidden layer during pre-training and a single linear layer during fine-tuning: “The classiﬁcation head is implemented by a MLP with one hidden layer at pre-training time and by a single linear layer at ﬁne-tuning time.” [S:d35d59fc5ce2#26]
- **DeiT — 2012.12877v2.pdf, p. 7:** The class branch is supervised by the true label, while the distillation branch is supervised by the teacher’s hard predicted label: “This distillation token is employed in a similar fashion as the class token, ex- cept that on output of the network its objective is to reproduce the (hard) label predicted by the teacher, instead of true label.” [S:cc5a543a8c6c#41]
- **DeiT — 2012.12877v2.pdf, p. 8:** At inference, separate linear classifiers act on the class and distillation embeddings, and late fusion adds their softmax outputs: “Yet our referent method is the late fusion of these two separate heads, for which we add the softmax output by the two classiﬁers to make the prediction.” [S:cc5a543a8c6c#46]

The papers agree that the class token’s output representation supports classification; DeiT adds a separately supervised distillation token and combines the two classifiers at inference. [S:d35d59fc5ce2#26] [S:cc5a543a8c6c#42] [S:cc5a543a8c6c#46]
